40 Questions to Ask Your Best Friend: Fun, Meaningful and Deeper Conversations

Use these fun and meaningful questions to ask your best friend to reconnect, share memories and learn what matters in each other’s lives today.

Good questions help best friends discover what has changed, revisit shared memories and understand what each person needs now. Start with light prompts, move to personal topics only when both people are comfortable, and answer the questions yourself too.

Friendship & Gratitude8–10 min readUpdated 7 November 2026
Written by RA FahimWishly Guide Editorial

Quick answer

Choose questions that suit the moment and your friend’s comfort. A mix of funny, memory-based and reflective prompts can make a conversation feel natural. Let either person skip a question and avoid turning a friendly chat into an interview.

  • Start with light questions before moving into personal topics.
  • Share your own answers so the conversation feels mutual.
  • Allow your friend to skip anything they do not want to discuss.

Fun questions to start the conversation

Light questions are useful when you are meeting after a busy week or want to make a video call feel less formal. They can lead to stories and laughter without asking someone to explain a difficult part of life.

Try asking one question, listening to the answer and following the story rather than moving quickly through a list.

  • What small thing made you laugh recently?
  • What food could you eat every week without getting tired of it?
  • If we had a free day and no plans, where would you want to go?
  • What is a skill you would learn just for fun?
  • Which song instantly reminds you of a particular year?
  • What is a harmless opinion you will defend forever?

Questions about shared memories

Friendship has a history, and looking back can remind you what you value about one another. Ask about an ordinary moment that became memorable, a trip, an inside joke or a time one of you showed up for the other.

Keep the questions open enough to invite a story. If a memory is painful or embarrassing, do not push the topic. The purpose is connection, not testing how much someone remembers.

  • What was your first impression of me?
  • Which ordinary day from our friendship do you remember most?
  • What inside joke still makes you laugh?
  • When did you first feel we had become close friends?
  • What is something we should do together again?
  • Which photo from our friendship deserves to be printed?

Questions about life right now

Best friends can know each other for years while missing important changes in everyday life. Ask what is taking most of their attention, what they are enjoying lately or what kind of support would be helpful this month.

Listen without immediately comparing experiences. You may have different schedules, priorities or challenges now. Showing interest in the person they are today is an important part of maintaining a long friendship.

  • What has been taking most of your energy lately?
  • What are you looking forward to this month?
  • What is something new you have learned about yourself?
  • What kind of weekend feels restorative to you now?
  • Is there a goal you would like someone to check in about?
  • What is one thing you wish you had more time for?

Deeper questions about the friendship

Ask deeper questions only when the setting feels comfortable and both people have time. A quiet walk or relaxed call may be better than a rushed conversation. Answer the questions yourself and be willing to hear something you did not expect.

If your friend says that something in the friendship has been difficult, listen before defending yourself. A question is an invitation to understand, not a demand for reassurance.

  • What makes you feel supported in a friendship?
  • Is there something you wish we did more often?
  • How do you prefer friends to check in when you are quiet?
  • What is one way I can be a better friend to you?
  • When do you feel most understood by people close to you?
  • What boundary helps you protect your time or energy?

Questions about the future and shared plans

Future-focused questions can turn a good conversation into a plan. Keep the ideas realistic and let your friend choose what they actually want. A shared wish does not need to become a promise or a fixed deadline.

You might choose one small thing to do together: a monthly call, a visit, a new recipe, a photo walk or a day trip. Put the plan on a calendar only if both people want that.

  • What place would you like us to visit together?
  • What tradition should we start this year?
  • What would a good year of friendship look like to you?
  • What skill or hobby would be fun to learn together?
  • What is one memory you hope we make in the next few years?
  • What kind of check-in would help us stay connected when life gets busy?

How to ask without making it feel like an interview

Choose one or two prompts, leave pauses and ask follow-up questions when your friend seems interested. You do not need to complete the list. Share your own story and let the conversation move in an unexpected direction.

If your friend seems tired, switch to something lighter or end the conversation warmly. A good question creates room for connection; it does not require someone to disclose more than they want.

Frequently asked questions

What are good questions to ask your best friend?

Ask about recent experiences, favourite memories, what they are looking forward to and what kind of support feels useful now.

What are deep questions to ask a close friend?

Ask what helps them feel understood, what they want more time for, what they have learned about themselves and how you can be a supportive friend.

How do I make a conversation with my best friend less awkward?

Start with a shared activity or light question, share your own answer and let the discussion move naturally rather than asking a long list in sequence.

Can I use these questions in a long-distance friendship?

Yes. Choose a few prompts for a call or message exchange, and allow time-zone and schedule differences when planning the conversation.
